<reason>A built a disciplined, consistent case around burden of proof: PRO must show the *magnitude* of treatment-attributable benefit exceeds harm, not merely that a mechanism is plausible or that untreated dysphoria is dangerous. A's sharpest move was exposing that PRO's suicide argument conflates the severity of an unmanaged risk with an established treatment effect on that risk — a point PRO never fully answered, instead repeatedly asserting mechanism plausibility and shifting the burden onto CON to prove an alternative superior. In the pressure round, A's answers were more substantive: A1 cleanly clarified that CON need not prove supportive care equivalent, only that PRO hasn't isolated its own causal contribution, and A2 supplied a concrete, falsifiable evidentiary standard, defusing PRO's "unfalsifiable by design" charge. PRO's answers to CON's questions were comparatively evasive, reasserting the mechanism/asymmetry framing rather than directly grappling with the causal-attribution problem. PRO's closing repeats the "uncertainty favors access" framing without engaging A's rebuttal that this is a policy tie-break rule, not evidence discharging PRO's burden as the resolution demands. B's clipped opening is also a minor execution cost. Overall A kept tighter control of the actual burden the motion imposes and answered pressure more directly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A2.1–A4.3), especially the point that PRO's own admission that suicide is a "background risk...plausibly reduced" undercuts treating suicide prevention as an established benefit rather than an assumed one, combined with A's direct, specific falsifiability answer that neutralized PRO's "unfalsifiable by design" pressure question.</best_rebuttal>
